title: Renal physiology — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Physiology Renal System lecture + syllabus

questions.stem: The kidneys are described as retroperitoneal, meaning they lie

options.label: A
options.text: behind the peritoneum on the posterior abdominal wall

options.label: B
options.text: within the peritoneal cavity among the intestines

options.label: C
options.text: inside the true pelvis below the bladder

options.label: D
options.text: within the thoracic cavity above the diaphragm

options.label: E
options.text: suspended freely in the greater omentum

questions.why: The kidneys sit behind the peritoneum against the posterior abdominal wall on either side of the vertebral column.

questions.stem: The right kidney normally lies slightly lower than the left because

options.label: A
options.text: the aorta displaces the left kidney up

options.label: B
options.text: the liver pushes the right kidney down

options.label: C
options.text: the spleen pushes the left kidney down

options.label: D
options.text: the right renal artery is longer

options.label: E
options.text: the right kidney is larger and heavier

questions.why: The bulk of the liver on the right displaces the right kidney a little caudally.

questions.stem: Urine formed in the kidney drains in the sequence

options.label: A
options.text: collecting duct, ureter, renal pelvis, calyx

options.label: B
options.text: renal pelvis, ureter, major calyx, bladder

options.label: C
options.text: minor calyx, major calyx, renal pelvis, ureter

options.label: D
options.text: renal pelvis, minor calyx, major calyx, ureter

options.label: E
options.text: major calyx, minor calyx, renal pelvis, ureter

questions.why: From a pyramid's apex, urine passes minor calyx to major calyx to renal pelvis, then into the ureter.

questions.stem: Each human kidney contains approximately how many nephrons?
questions.why: There are roughly 1.25 million nephrons per kidney.

questions.stem: Juxtamedullary nephrons, about 15% of the total, differ from cortical nephrons in that they have

options.label: A
options.text: short loops of Henle confined to the cortex

options.label: B
options.text: no loop of Henle at all

options.label: C
options.text: glomeruli located in the outer cortex

options.label: E
options.text: long loops of Henle that dip deep into the medulla

questions.why: Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops extending into the pyramids, essential for concentrating urine; cortical nephrons (≈85%) have short loops.

questions.stem: The vasa recta, the hairpin capillaries running alongside the loop of Henle, arise from the efferent arterioles of
questions.why: Vasa recta come specifically from juxtamedullary efferent arterioles and serve the countercurrent exchanger.

questions.stem: Within the juxtaglomerular apparatus, the cells that actually produce and secrete renin are the

options.label: A
options.text: principal cells of the collecting duct

options.label: B
options.text: granular cells of the afferent arteriole

options.label: C
options.text: macula densa cells of the distal tubule

questions.why: Granular cells are modified smooth muscle in the afferent arteriole wall and secrete renin.

questions.stem: The macula densa, part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, functions to

options.label: A
options.text: reabsorb glucose in the proximal tubule

options.label: C
options.text: sense the NaCl in the distal tubular fluid

options.label: D
options.text: secrete renin into the afferent arteriole

questions.why: Macula densa cells in the distal tubule wall monitor luminal NaCl and drive tubuloglomerular feedback.

questions.stem: Besides producing renin and erythropoietin, the kidney contributes to mineral homeostasis by

options.label: D
options.text: converting vitamin D to its active form

questions.why: The kidney performs the final hydroxylation that activates vitamin D (to calcitriol).

questions.stem: The yellow colour of normal urine is due mainly to the pigment
questions.why: Urochrome/urobilin, a product of haemoglobin destruction, gives urine its yellow colour.

questions.stem: Urine that has been left to stand develops an ammonia smell because
questions.why: Bacterial metabolism of urea on standing releases ammonia.

questions.stem: A sweet or fruity odour of the urine suggests the presence of

options.label: C
options.text: excess urea from a high-protein diet

questions.why: Ketone bodies in diabetic ketoacidosis give urine a sweet, fruity smell.

questions.stem: The solute present in the highest concentration in normal urine is
questions.why: Urea (~9.3 g/L) is the most concentrated normal urinary solute, ahead of chloride, sodium, potassium and creatinine.

questions.stem: The specific gravity of normal urine ranges approximately from
questions.why: Normal urine specific gravity lies between about 1.001 and 1.035, reflecting its solute load.

questions.stem: The smooth muscle of the bladder wall responsible for expelling urine is the
questions.why: The detrusor is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall whose contraction empties the bladder.

questions.stem: The external urethral sphincter differs from the internal one in that it is

options.label: A
options.text: voluntary skeletal muscle via the pudendal nerve

options.label: C
options.text: smooth muscle controlled by the pelvic nerve

options.label: D
options.text: cardiac muscle supplied by the vagus

options.label: E
options.text: formed from the detrusor muscle itself

questions.why: The external sphincter is skeletal muscle controlled voluntarily through the pudendal nerve (motor neurons in Onuf's nucleus).

questions.stem: Parasympathetic fibres reaching the bladder through the pelvic nerves (S2-S4) act to

options.label: A
options.text: contract only the external urethral sphincter

options.label: B
options.text: contract the detrusor and relax the internal sphincter

options.label: C
options.text: relax the detrusor and contract the internal sphincter

options.label: D
options.text: contract both the detrusor and the internal sphincter

options.label: E
options.text: relax both the detrusor and the internal sphincter

questions.why: Parasympathetic activity empties the bladder: detrusor contraction with sphincter relaxation.

questions.stem: Sympathetic fibres in the hypogastric nerve (T12-L2) promote urine storage by

options.label: B
options.text: relaxing both detrusor and internal sphincter

options.label: C
options.text: relaxing the detrusor and contracting the bladder neck

options.label: D
options.text: contracting the detrusor and relaxing the bladder neck

questions.why: Sympathetic outflow relaxes the detrusor (β) and contracts the internal sphincter (α), favouring filling and storage.

questions.stem: The supraspinal centre that coordinates the micturition reflex is located in the
questions.why: The pontine micturition centre (Barrington's centre) coordinates voiding via the sacral cord.

questions.stem: After normal voiding, the adult bladder typically retains a residual volume of about
questions.why: The bladder holds about 500 ml and leaves roughly 50 ml residual after voiding.

questions.stem: The glomerular filtration barrier, from blood to capsular space, consists of the

options.label: A
options.text: fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane and podocyte slits

options.label: B
options.text: transitional epithelium, muscle layer and serosa

options.label: D
options.text: macula densa, mesangium and granular cells

options.label: E
options.text: brush border, basolateral membrane and tight junctions

questions.why: Filtrate crosses the fenestrated capillary endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane, and the filtration slits between podocyte pedicels.

questions.stem: The negative charge carried by all three layers of the filtration barrier mainly acts to

options.label: A
options.text: reverse the direction of filtrate flow

options.label: B
options.text: retard the filtration of anionic molecules

options.label: C
options.text: attract and filter small cations preferentially

options.label: D
options.text: prevent water from crossing the membrane

options.label: E
options.text: increase the filtration of plasma proteins

questions.why: The fixed negative charge repels anions such as albumin, helping keep the filtrate protein-free.

questions.stem: Net filtration pressure in the glomerulus is calculated as glomerular hydrostatic pressure minus the sum of blood oncotic and capsular pressures, giving roughly
questions.why: NFP = GBHP - (BCOP + CHP) = 55 - (30 + 15) = 10 mmHg.

questions.stem: The unusually high glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (about 55 mmHg) results from

options.label: A
options.text: the low resistance of the peritubular capillaries

options.label: B
options.text: the absence of a venous drainage from the glomerulus

options.label: C
options.text: direct connection of the glomerulus to the aorta

options.label: D
options.text: the efferent arteriole being narrower than the afferent

options.label: E
options.text: the afferent arteriole being narrower than the efferent

questions.why: A wider afferent and narrower efferent arteriole maintain a high pressure within the glomerular tuft.

questions.stem: A normal glomerular filtration rate of about 125 ml/min amounts to roughly how much filtrate per day?
questions.why: About 125 ml/min comes to roughly 180 L/day, of which ~99% is reabsorbed.

questions.stem: Renal autoregulation keeps GFR nearly constant over a mean arterial pressure range of about
questions.why: Autoregulation holds GFR steady between roughly 80 and 180 mmHg.

questions.stem: The myogenic mechanism of renal autoregulation works because a rise in arterial pressure

options.label: A
options.text: stimulates renin release from granular cells

options.label: B
options.text: stretches the afferent arteriole, which then contracts

options.label: C
options.text: relaxes the afferent arteriole, increasing flow

options.label: D
options.text: dilates the efferent arteriole to drop pressure

options.label: E
options.text: closes the macula densa feedback loop

questions.why: Stretch of the afferent arteriole triggers reflex smooth-muscle contraction, offsetting the pressure rise.

questions.stem: In tubuloglomerular feedback, a rise in distal tubular NaCl detected by the macula densa leads to

options.label: A
options.text: renin release that raises systemic pressure

options.label: C
options.text: afferent arteriolar constriction that lowers GFR back to normal

options.label: D
options.text: afferent arteriolar dilatation that raises GFR further

options.label: E
options.text: efferent arteriolar constriction that raises GFR

questions.why: High luminal NaCl makes the macula densa release ATP/adenosine, constricting the afferent arteriole and returning GFR toward normal.

questions.stem: Renal clearance of a substance is defined as the

options.label: A
options.text: fraction of the substance reabsorbed in the tubule

options.label: B
options.text: rate at which urine is formed by the glomeruli

options.label: C
options.text: concentration of the substance in the final urine

options.label: D
options.text: volume of plasma completely cleared of it per unit time

options.label: E
options.text: mass of the substance filtered per minute

questions.why: Clearance (RC = UV/P) is the plasma volume cleared of a substance per minute.

questions.stem: Inulin is the ideal marker of GFR because it is

options.label: A
options.text: freely filtered and almost completely reabsorbed

options.label: B
options.text: secreted so heavily that none appears in blood

options.label: C
options.text: bound to plasma proteins and not filtered

options.label: D
options.text: produced endogenously at a constant rate

options.label: E
options.text: freely filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted

questions.why: Inulin's clearance equals GFR because it is filtered and then neither reabsorbed nor secreted.

questions.stem: If the clearance of a substance is greater than that of inulin, the substance must be
questions.why: A clearance above inulin's means net tubular secretion adds the substance to the filtrate.

questions.stem: Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is used to estimate renal plasma flow because it is

options.label: A
options.text: bound to red cells rather than plasma

options.label: B
options.text: almost completely cleared in a single pass

options.label: C
options.text: entirely reabsorbed so none is excreted

options.label: D
options.text: filtered but not secreted at all

questions.why: PAH is filtered (~20%) and secreted (~80%), so nearly all is removed in one pass, approximating renal plasma flow.

questions.stem: Creatinine is commonly used instead of inulin to estimate GFR clinically because it is

options.label: A
options.text: entirely secreted by the distal tubule

options.label: B
options.text: bound to plasma proteins and unfiltered

options.label: C
options.text: endogenous, filtered and only slightly secreted

options.label: D
options.text: not present in the body unless infused

options.label: E
options.text: heavily reabsorbed in the proximal tubule

questions.why: Endogenous creatinine is freely filtered and only slightly secreted (~10% excess), giving a convenient GFR estimate.

questions.stem: Renal blood flow is obtained from renal plasma flow using the haematocrit by the relation
questions.why: Plasma is the fraction (1 - Hct) of blood, so RBF = RPF / (1 - Hct).

questions.stem: Across the whole nephron, roughly what proportion of the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed back into the blood?
questions.why: Around 99% of the ~180 L filtered daily is reabsorbed, leaving about 1-2 L of urine.

questions.stem: Sodium reabsorption consumes about 80% of the kidney's energy because it depends on the

options.label: D
options.text: aquaporin channels of the collecting duct

options.label: E
options.text: Cl-/HCO3- exchanger in the proximal tubule

questions.why: Basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase actively pumps Na+ out of the cell, creating the gradient that drives most tubular transport.

questions.stem: Unlike glucose, the reabsorption of sodium does not show a transport maximum because it

options.label: A
options.text: relies on a single low-capacity carrier

options.label: B
options.text: it is pumped all along the tubule

options.label: C
options.text: is reabsorbed only in the proximal tubule

questions.why: Na+ is handled all along the tubule by abundant pumps, so it has no single saturable Tm like glucose.

questions.stem: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs approximately what fraction of filtered sodium and water?
questions.why: The PCT reabsorbs roughly 65% of filtered Na+ and water (and essentially all glucose and amino acids).

questions.stem: Glucose, amino acids and most organic nutrients are reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by

options.label: A
options.text: primary active transport using their own ATPases

options.label: D
options.text: secondary active cotransport coupled to sodium

options.label: E
options.text: simple diffusion down their own gradients

questions.why: These solutes are cotransported with Na+ as it moves down its gradient — secondary active transport.

questions.stem: A transport maximum sets a renal threshold because

options.label: A
options.text: the substance can no longer be filtered at the glomerulus

options.label: B
options.text: the tubule stops reabsorbing water as well

options.label: C
options.text: secretion into the lumen ceases entirely

options.label: D
options.text: the substance is destroyed within the tubule cell

options.label: E
options.text: once the carriers are saturated, the excess substance is excreted

questions.why: When carrier proteins are saturated at the Tm, any filtered load above that spills into the urine.

questions.stem: The descending limb of the loop of Henle is characterised by being

options.label: A
options.text: permeable to water but not to solute

options.label: B
options.text: permeable to solute but not to water

options.label: C
options.text: permeable to both water and solute equally

options.label: D
options.text: impermeable to both water and solute

options.label: E
options.text: the main site of active Na+ pumping

questions.why: Water leaves the water-permeable descending limb osmotically, while solute stays, concentrating the filtrate toward the bend.

questions.stem: The main luminal carrier bringing sodium into the cells of the thick ascending limb is the
questions.why: The thick ascending limb uses the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (the target of loop diuretics).

questions.stem: At the bend of the loop of Henle in a juxtamedullary nephron, the tubular fluid reaches an osmolality of about
questions.why: Water loss along the descending limb concentrates the fluid to about 1200 mOsm at the hairpin tip.

questions.stem: By the time tubular fluid reaches the early distal convoluted tubule it is hypotonic (about 100 mOsm) because the ascending limb has

options.label: A
options.text: secreted extra solute into the lumen

options.label: B
options.text: added aquaporins to let water in

options.label: D
options.text: pumped out NaCl while impermeable to water

questions.why: The water-impermeable ascending limb removes NaCl, diluting the fluid to about 100 mOsm.

questions.stem: The vasa recta act as a countercurrent exchanger that chiefly serves to

options.label: A
options.text: generate the medullary gradient by pumping NaCl

options.label: B
options.text: filter plasma a second time in the medulla

options.label: C
options.text: secrete renin in response to low flow

options.label: D
options.text: reabsorb all the glucose escaping the PCT

questions.why: The hairpin vasa recta supply the medulla yet, by countercurrent exchange, avoid washing out its hypertonicity.

questions.stem: Antidiuretic hormone concentrates the urine by

options.label: A
options.text: inserting aquaporins into the collecting duct

options.label: B
options.text: pumping sodium out of the ascending limb

questions.why: ADH (vasopressin) acts via cAMP to insert aquaporins into collecting-duct principal cells, raising water reabsorption.

questions.stem: The stimulus that most directly triggers ADH release is

options.label: A
options.text: a rise in arterial oxygen tension

options.label: D
options.text: a rise in distal tubular NaCl

questions.why: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect rising osmolality and drive posterior-pituitary release of ADH (angiotensin II also stimulates it).

questions.stem: The high blood glucose of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus produces an osmotic diuresis because glucose

options.label: C
options.text: exceeds its Tm and holds water in the tubule

questions.why: Once filtered glucose exceeds the reabsorptive Tm, the unreabsorbed glucose osmotically retains water in the tubule.

questions.stem: Furosemide (lasix) produces diuresis by inhibiting the

options.label: B
options.text: carbonic anhydrase of the proximal tubule

options.label: C
options.text: epithelial Na+ channel of the distal tubule

options.label: D
options.text: Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter of the thick ascending limb

options.label: E
options.text: Na+-glucose cotransporter of the proximal tubule

questions.why: Loop diuretics block the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the medullary thick ascending limb.

questions.stem: Alcohol promotes diuresis mainly by

options.label: A
options.text: blocking sodium reabsorption in the loop

options.label: C
options.text: acting as a non-reabsorbed osmotic agent

options.label: E
options.text: inhibiting the secretion of antidiuretic hormone

questions.why: Alcohol suppresses ADH release, reducing collecting-duct water reabsorption.

questions.stem: Potassium is handled along the nephron such that it is

options.label: A
options.text: reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and secreted in the distal tubule

options.label: B
options.text: secreted in the proximal tubule and reabsorbed distally

options.label: E
options.text: reabsorbed equally along the whole tubule

questions.why: K+ is reabsorbed unregulated in the PCT and secreted, under aldosterone control, in the distal tubule and collecting duct.

questions.stem: Renin released from the kidney acts on its substrate to produce
questions.why: Renin converts liver-derived angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

questions.stem: Angiotensin-converting enzyme, which forms angiotensin II from angiotensin I, is found chiefly in the
questions.why: ACE in the lungs converts angiotensin I to the active angiotensin II.

questions.stem: Which action is NOT produced by angiotensin II?
questions.why: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor, not a vasodilator; it also drives thirst, aldosterone, ADH and mesangial contraction.

questions.stem: Aldosterone acts on the distal nephron to

options.label: E
options.text: reabsorb sodium and water, secrete potassium

questions.why: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex increases Na+ (and water) reabsorption and K+ secretion in the distal tubule and collecting duct.

questions.stem: Atrial natriuretic peptide opposes the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system by
questions.why: ANP promotes natriuresis and diuresis, lowering blood volume and opposing RAAS.

questions.stem: Renin secretion by the granular cells is stimulated by

options.label: B
options.text: a fall in renal perfusion pressure

options.label: E
options.text: a high distal tubular NaCl load

questions.why: Low perfusion pressure, sympathetic drive and low macula densa NaCl all stimulate renin release.

questions.stem: The kidneys keep the osmotic concentration of body fluids close to
questions.why: Plasma osmolality is held near 300 mOsm by regulated water and solute handling.

questions.stem: A convenient physiological way to view acid-base handling is that reabsorbing a bicarbonate ion is equivalent to
questions.why: Because HCO3- buffers H+, reclaiming HCO3- is equivalent to removing H+ (and losing HCO3- equals gaining H+).

questions.stem: The most important buffer system of the blood plasma (extracellular fluid) is the
questions.why: The bicarbonate/carbonic acid pair is the principal ECF buffer; phosphate dominates urine and ICF, protein the cells.

questions.stem: The phosphate buffer system is most important as a buffer of the
questions.why: Phosphate is concentrated in urine and cells, where it buffers effectively; it is minor in plasma.

questions.stem: Proteins such as haemoglobin can buffer both acids and bases because they are

options.label: A
options.text: unable to change charge with pH

options.label: B
options.text: amphoteric - they donate and accept H+

options.label: D
options.text: strong bases that bind all H+

questions.why: Amino acid side groups let proteins release or take up H+ depending on pH, making them amphoteric buffers.

questions.stem: Movement of bicarbonate out of the red cell in exchange for chloride, during CO2 transport, is known as the
questions.why: The HCO3-/Cl- antiport across the red-cell membrane is the chloride shift, or Hamburger effect.

questions.stem: Only the kidney can rid the body of which type of acid?

options.label: C
options.text: all acids are handled by the lungs

questions.why: The lungs excrete the volatile acid (CO2); only the kidneys eliminate fixed, non-volatile acids.

questions.stem: Reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate in the proximal tubule depends on secretion of H+, which in the lumen

options.label: B
options.text: is excreted unchanged as free acid

options.label: D
options.text: is reabsorbed together with the bicarbonate

options.label: E
options.text: joins HCO3- to form CO2 and water

questions.why: Secreted H+ joins filtered HCO3- to make H2CO3, which becomes CO2 + H2O; these enter the cell and regenerate HCO3- for reabsorption.

questions.stem: Generation of new bicarbonate linked to ammonium excretion uses the amino acid
questions.why: Tubular metabolism of glutamine produces two NH4+ (excreted) and two new HCO3- (added to blood) per molecule.

questions.stem: In a patient with respiratory acidosis the typical arterial picture is

options.label: A
options.text: pH normal with a low PaCO2 and low bicarbonate

options.label: B
options.text: pH below 7.35 with a raised PaCO2 and initially normal bicarbonate

options.label: C
options.text: pH above 7.45 with a low PaCO2

options.label: D
options.text: pH below 7.35 with a low bicarbonate and normal PaCO2

options.label: E
options.text: pH above 7.45 with a raised bicarbonate

questions.why: Hypoventilation retains CO2: pH < 7.35, PaCO2 > 45 mmHg, with bicarbonate normal until renal compensation.

questions.stem: Metabolic acidosis (for example from diabetic ketoacidosis) is characterised by

options.label: A
options.text: a normal bicarbonate with a low PaCO2

options.label: B
options.text: a raised bicarbonate with a raised PaCO2

options.label: C
options.text: a low bicarbonate with a normal PaCO2

options.label: D
options.text: a raised PaCO2 with a normal bicarbonate

options.label: E
options.text: a raised bicarbonate with a low PaCO2

questions.why: Metabolic acidosis lowers HCO3- below 22 mEq/L while PaCO2 stays normal until respiratory compensation begins.

questions.stem: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis occurs within minutes and consists of

options.label: D
options.text: increased ventilation that drives off CO2

questions.why: The lungs hyperventilate to blow off CO2, restoring the HCO3-/H2CO3 ratio toward 20:1 within minutes.

questions.stem: The absolute blood pH limits compatible with life are approximately
questions.why: Survival is possible only within a pH of roughly 7.0 to 7.8; beyond these, coma or tetany and death follow.

questions.stem: In the collecting duct, the cells that secrete bicarbonate during alkalosis are the
questions.why: Type B intercalated cells secrete HCO3- (and reabsorb H+) in alkalosis, the reverse of type A cells.
